title: Chapter 5: Elasticity: Responsiveness of Demand and Supply

questions.topic: Price Elasticity of Demand vs. Raw Slope
questions.title: Why Economists Measure Elasticity with Percentage Changes
questions.prompt_template: Why do economists measure consumer price sensitivity using percentage changes (elasticity) rather than the raw slope of a demand curve?

hints.text: Consider what happens to the numerical slope if you measure price in cents instead of dollars or coffee in ounces instead of cups.
Elasticity removes arbitrary measurement units so responsiveness can be compared consistently across completely different markets.

options_template.text: Percentage changes produce a unit-free measure that does not change when measurement units (such as dollars vs. cents or cups vs. ounces) are altered.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because percentage changes cancel out measurement units, elasticity lets economists compare responsiveness across different goods on one standardized scale.

options_template.text: Raw slope is always positive for demand curves, whereas percentage changes automatically make demand elasticity negative.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal): Downward-sloping demand curves already have a negative raw slope; the unit-free property—not the sign—is why economists use percentage changes.

options_template.text: Percentage changes guarantee that elasticity stays constant at every single point along a straight-line demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Elasticity Conflation): A straight-line demand curve has a constant raw slope, whereas its price elasticity changes at every point along the line.

options_template.text: Raw slope cannot be calculated for linear demand equations, whereas percentage changes require no price or quantity data.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Formula Misconception): Raw slope is trivially computed for linear demand curves, and elasticity still requires price and quantity observations.

questions.title: Defining Inelastic Demand Under the Absolute Value Convention
questions.prompt_template: Using the standard absolute value convention for own-price elasticity of demand ($|\varepsilon_d|$), which statement accurately characterizes inelastic demand?

hints.text: Compare the size of the percentage change in quantity demanded to the size of the percentage change in price.
Inelastic demand means buyers are relatively unresponsive to price changes, so the numerator is smaller than the denominator.

options_template.text: $|\varepsilon_d| > 1$, meaning the percentage change in quantity demanded is larger than the percentage change in price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Regime Reversal): $|\varepsilon_d| > 1$ defines elastic demand, where consumers respond more than proportionally to price changes.

options_template.text: $|\varepsilon_d| < 1$, meaning the percentage change in quantity demanded is smaller than the percentage change in price.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When $|\varepsilon_d| < 1$, quantity demanded responds less than proportionally to a price change, indicating relatively unresponsive (inelastic) demand.

options_template.text: $|\varepsilon_d| = 1$, meaning quantity demanded does not change at all when price changes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unit-Elastic vs. Perfectly Inelastic Confusion): $|\varepsilon_d| = 1$ means percentage changes in quantity and price are equal (unit elastic), whereas zero quantity response corresponds to $|\varepsilon_d| = 0$.

options_template.text: $\varepsilon_d > 0$, meaning consumers buy more of the good whenever its price increases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Law of Demand Violation): For ordinary downward-sloping demand, raw $\varepsilon_d$ is negative; inelasticity refers to a magnitude $|\varepsilon_d| < 1$, not a positive slope.

questions.title: Purpose of the Midpoint Formula in Elasticity Calculations
questions.prompt_template: Why do economists use the midpoint (arc) formula rather than the standard initial-value percentage-change formula when computing elasticity between two points on a demand curve?

hints.text: Think about what happens to a standard percentage change when price rises from $\$80$ to $\$100$ versus falling from $\$100$ to $\$80$.
Dividing each change by the average of the starting and ending values eliminates dependence on which point is treated as the starting base.

options_template.text: It eliminates direction bias so the elasticity between Point A and Point B is identical whether price rises from A to B or falls from B to A.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Using the midpoint average as the base ensures symmetry, giving the same elasticity value regardless of the direction of movement between two points.

options_template.text: It converts every nonlinear demand curve into a straight line with a constant slope.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Geometric Distortion): The midpoint formula standardizes the percentage base between two discrete points; it does not alter the underlying shape of the demand curve.

options_template.text: It guarantees that the resulting price elasticity of demand will always equal $1.0$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Midpoint-Unit-Elastic Conflation): The geometric midpoint of a full linear demand curve happens to be unit elastic, but the midpoint formula between any two arbitrary points can yield elastic, unit-elastic, or inelastic values.

options_template.text: It allows economists to ignore quantity changes and compute elasticity solely from average prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Quantity Response): The midpoint formula requires both midpoint percentage changes—$\%\Delta Q_d$ in the numerator and $\%\Delta P$ in the denominator.

questions.topic: Determinants of Price Elasticity of Demand
questions.title: Structural Factors That Increase Demand Elasticity
questions.prompt_template: Holding other factors constant, which structural condition tends to make consumer demand for a good MORE price elastic?

hints.text: Recall the four determinants of price elasticity of demand: substitutes, necessity vs. discretionary use, budget share, and time horizon.
Ask which condition gives buyers the greatest ability and incentive to switch away when the price rises.

options_template.text: The good is a medically necessary treatment with virtually no clinically appropriate alternatives.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Determinant Reversal): Few close substitutes and high necessity limit buyers' ability to cut back, making demand more inelastic rather than more elastic.

options_template.text: The good accounts for a tiny fraction of a household's monthly budget.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Budget Share Reversal): When an item takes up a tiny budget share, a percentage price hike barely affects household spending, tending to make demand less elastic.

options_template.text: Buyers have many close substitutes available and a longer time horizon to adjust their purchasing habits.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Readily available close substitutes and a longer adjustment period allow buyers to switch away more easily, increasing price elasticity of demand.

options_template.text: Consumers must decide immediately with no time to search for alternative products.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Time-Horizon Reversal): A shorter time horizon restricts substitution and adjustment, making demand more inelastic in the short run.

questions.title: Economic Meaning of Perfectly Inelastic Demand
questions.prompt_template: What does a price elasticity of demand equal to zero ($|\varepsilon_d| = 0$) indicate about consumer behavior?

hints.text: Look at the ratio $\varepsilon_d = \%\Delta Q_d / \%\Delta P$: what must the numerator equal for the fraction to be zero?
Zero elasticity is the extreme polar limit where quantity demanded shows zero responsiveness to price changes.

options_template.text: Quantity demanded falls to zero if the seller raises price by even one cent.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Polar-Extreme Swap): Losing all buyers from any tiny price increase describes perfectly elastic demand ($|\varepsilon_d| = \infty$), not $|\varepsilon_d| = 0$.

options_template.text: Consumers change quantity demanded by the exact same percentage as any price change.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unit-Elastic Confusion): Equal percentage changes in quantity and price define unit elastic demand ($|\varepsilon_d| = 1$), not $|\varepsilon_d| = 0$.

options_template.text: Total revenue remains completely constant whenever price increases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Invariance Confusion): Constant total revenue occurs under unit elastic demand ($|\varepsilon_d| = 1$); under perfectly inelastic demand, higher price raises total revenue proportionally.

options_template.text: Quantity demanded remains completely unchanged regardless of changes in price.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When $|\varepsilon_d| = 0$ (perfectly inelastic demand), $\%\Delta Q_d = 0$ for any $\%\Delta P$, meaning buyers purchase the same quantity regardless of price.

questions.title: Price Effect vs. Quantity Effect During a Price Increase
questions.prompt_template: When a firm raises the price of its product along a downward-sloping demand curve, how do the price effect and the quantity effect influence Total Revenue ($TR = P \times Q$)?

hints.text: Break $TR = P \times Q$ into two opposing forces: higher dollars per unit sold versus fewer total units sold.
Raising price pushes $P$ up while pulling $Q$ down; total revenue changes based on which force is larger.

options_template.text: Both the price effect and the quantity effect push total revenue upward whenever price rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring the Law of Demand): Raising price reduces quantity demanded along a downward-sloping demand curve, so the quantity effect pulls total revenue downward.

options_template.text: The price effect and quantity effect always cancel out exactly, leaving total revenue unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overgeneralizing Unit Elasticity): The two effects cancel out only when demand is unit elastic ($|\varepsilon_d| = 1$); otherwise one effect dominates.

options_template.text: The price effect pulls total revenue downward, while the quantity effect pushes total revenue upward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Forces): During a price increase, higher $P$ raises revenue per unit (positive price effect) and lower $Q$ reduces total units sold (negative quantity effect)—not the reverse.

options_template.text: The price effect pushes total revenue upward (more revenue per remaining unit sold), while the quantity effect pulls total revenue downward (fewer units sold).
options_template.feedback: Correct. A price hike creates a tug-of-war: each remaining unit brings in more dollars (positive price effect), while lost unit sales reduce revenue (negative quantity effect).

questions.title: Applying the Total Revenue Test to a Price Cut
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a seller lowers its price and observes that Total Revenue ($TR = P \times Q$) decreases over that price interval. According to the Total Revenue Test, what must be true about demand over that interval?

hints.text: Check whether price and total revenue moved in the same direction or opposite directions.
When price and total revenue move in the same direction ($P \downarrow$ and $TR \downarrow$), the price effect dominates the quantity effect.

options_template.text: Demand is elastic ($|\varepsilon_d| > 1$) because the quantity gain outweighed the price cut.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Mismatch): If demand were elastic, a price cut would trigger a larger percentage jump in quantity and cause total revenue to rise, not fall.

options_template.text: Demand is unit elastic ($|\varepsilon_d| = 1$) because revenue moved proportionally with price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unit-Elastic Misinterpretation): Under unit elastic demand, total revenue stays unchanged when price changes rather than falling.

options_template.text: Demand is inelastic ($|\varepsilon_d| < 1$) because price and total revenue moved in the same direction.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When $P$ falls and $TR$ also falls, buyers did not expand purchases enough to offset the lower price per unit—confirming inelastic demand ($|\varepsilon_d| < 1$).

options_template.text: Demand must be upward-sloping because lowering price reduced dollar sales.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Confusing $Q$ with $TR$): Along a normal downward-sloping demand curve, quantity demanded still rises when price falls; total revenue falls whenever that quantity gain is smaller in percentage terms than the price drop.

questions.title: Elasticity Condition at Maximum Total Revenue
questions.prompt_template: Before accounting for production costs, at what price elasticity of demand does a firm facing a downward-sloping linear demand curve reach its maximum Total Revenue?

hints.text: Think about whether the firm can still raise $TR$ by cutting price in the elastic region or raising price in the inelastic region.
Revenue stops climbing and reaches its peak at the exact boundary between the elastic and inelastic regions.

options_template.text: At the unit-elastic midpoint where $|\varepsilon_d| = 1$.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Along a linear demand curve, total revenue rises as price falls through the elastic region, peaks at the unit-elastic midpoint ($|\varepsilon_d| = 1$), and falls in the inelastic region.

options_template.text: At the vertical price intercept where $|\varepsilon_d| = \infty$ and price is highest.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Max Price = Max Revenue): At the vertical intercept, quantity sold is zero, so $TR = P \times 0 = \$0$.

options_template.text: At the horizontal quantity intercept where $|\varepsilon_d| = 0$ and quantity sold is largest.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Max Quantity = Max Revenue): At the horizontal intercept, price is zero, so $TR = \$0 \times Q = \$0$.

options_template.text: Anywhere in the inelastic region ($|\varepsilon_d| < 1$) because buyers are insensitive to price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Incomplete Optimization): In the inelastic region, raising price increases total revenue, so revenue cannot yet be maximized until price rises up to the unit-elastic point ($|\varepsilon_d| = 1$).

questions.title: Why Economists Preserve the Sign of Income Elasticity
questions.prompt_template: Why must economists retain the plus or minus sign when reporting the income elasticity of demand ($\varepsilon_I$) rather than taking its absolute value?

hints.text: Contrast own-price elasticity (where the Law of Demand implies a negative sign) with income elasticity (where demand can move either way when income rises).
Recall how $\varepsilon_I > 0$ and $\varepsilon_I < 0$ classify two distinct types of goods.

options_template.text: Because the sign distinguishes elastic goods from inelastic goods along a single demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Magnitude vs. Sign Confusion): Whether a good is income-elastic or income-inelastic depends on whether $|\varepsilon_I|$ exceeds $1$, whereas the sign distinguishes normal from inferior goods.

options_template.text: Because taking the absolute value would erase the distinction between normal goods ($\varepsilon_I > 0$) and inferior goods ($\varepsilon_I < 0$).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Unlike own-price elasticity, income elasticity can be positive (normal goods) or negative (inferior goods); dropping the sign destroys that economic classification.

options_template.text: Because income elasticity is always negative by the Law of Demand.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Law of Demand Misapplication): The Law of Demand applies to own-price changes, not income changes; most goods are normal goods with $\varepsilon_I > 0$.

options_template.text: Because the sign indicates whether the two goods in question are substitutes or complements.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Income vs. Cross-Price Confusion): Substitutes and complements are identified by the sign of cross-price elasticity ($\varepsilon_{xy}$), not income elasticity ($\varepsilon_I$).

questions.title: Classifying a Good with Positive Income Elasticity Below One
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a stylized empirical estimate shows that a household's income elasticity of demand for basic groceries is $\varepsilon_I = +0.45$. How is this good classified?

hints.text: First check the sign ($+$ vs. $-$) to determine whether the good is normal or inferior.
Next check whether the magnitude is between $0$ and $1$ (necessity) or greater than $1$ (luxury).

options_template.text: An inferior good, because $\varepsilon_I$ is less than $1$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Threshold Confusion): Inferior goods require a negative income elasticity ($\varepsilon_I < 0$), not simply a value less than $1$.

options_template.text: A normal luxury good, because $\varepsilon_I$ is positive.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Necessity vs. Luxury Confusion): While $\varepsilon_I > 0$ confirms a normal good, a luxury requires $\varepsilon_I > 1$ (spending rises faster than income).

options_template.text: A normal necessity (income-inelastic normal good), because $0 < \varepsilon_I < 1$.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The positive sign confirms a normal good (demand rises with income), and $0.45 < 1$ shows demand rises less than proportionally with income, defining a normal necessity.

options_template.text: A complementary good, because $\varepsilon_I$ lies between $0$ and $1$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elasticity Type Confusion): Complements are classified by negative cross-price elasticity ($\varepsilon_{xy} < 0$), not by income elasticity.

questions.title: Interpreting a Negative Cross-Price Elasticity
questions.prompt_template: If the cross-price elasticity of demand between Good $X$ and Good $Y$ is negative ($\varepsilon_{xy} < 0$), what economic relationship exists between the two goods?

hints.text: Write out the definition $\varepsilon_{xy} = \%\Delta Q_x / \%\Delta P_y$: for the ratio to be negative, $P_y$ and $Q_x$ must move in opposite directions.
Think of goods consumed together—like game consoles and video games, or espresso shots and oat milk.

options_template.text: Good $X$ and Good $Y$ are substitutes, because a higher price for $Y$ causes consumers to buy more of $X$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal for Related Goods): Substitutes move together ($P_y \uparrow \Rightarrow Q_x \uparrow$), giving a positive cross-price elasticity ($\varepsilon_{xy} > 0$).

options_template.text: Good $X$ and Good $Y$ are unrelated goods whose markets do not interact.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero vs. Negative Confusion): Unrelated goods have a cross-price elasticity equal to zero ($\varepsilon_{xy} = 0$), not negative.

options_template.text: Good $X$ is an inferior good whenever Good $Y$ becomes more expensive.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Income vs. Cross-Price Conflation): Inferior goods are defined by negative income elasticity ($\varepsilon_I < 0$), not negative cross-price elasticity.

options_template.text: Good $X$ and Good $Y$ are complements, because a higher price for $Y$ reduces the quantity demanded of $X$.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A negative $\varepsilon_{xy}$ means $P_y$ and $Q_x$ move in opposite directions—the hallmark of complementary goods consumed together.

questions.title: Production Conditions Associated with Highly Inelastic Supply
questions.prompt_template: Which market characteristic is most closely associated with a highly inelastic price elasticity of supply ($\varepsilon_s \approx 0$)?

hints.text: Recall what governs supply elasticity: production capacity constraints and the time horizon available to adjust output.
Compare digital downloads or mass-produced apparel with beachfront land or crops immediately after harvest.

options_template.text: Output can be replicated instantly at nearly constant marginal cost, such as digital software downloads.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elastic vs. Inelastic Supply Reversal): Instant, low-cost scaling allows huge quantity responses to price changes, producing highly elastic supply ($\varepsilon_s > 1$).

options_template.text: Consumers have numerous close substitutes for the product.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand vs. Supply Determinant Swap): Availability of consumer substitutes determines demand elasticity ($\varepsilon_d$), not supply elasticity ($\varepsilon_s$).

options_template.text: Firms have many years to construct new factories and enter the industry.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Time-Horizon Reversal): Long-run entry and factory expansion make supply much more elastic, not inelastic.

options_template.text: Production capacity is fixed in the immediate market period or relies on non-reproducible inputs such as beachfront land.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When capacity cannot be expanded quickly (e.g., harvested crops in the immediate period or fixed beachfront parcels), quantity supplied barely responds to price, yielding $\varepsilon_s \approx 0$.

questions.title: What Governs the Economic Burden of an Excise Tax
questions.prompt_template: In a standard competitive market with a per-unit excise tax (assuming no differences in compliance or transaction costs), what determines how the economic burden of the tax is split between buyers and sellers?

hints.text: Distinguish statutory incidence (who writes the check to the government) from economic incidence (who loses surplus through price changes).
Think about which side of the market has fewer alternatives and therefore cannot easily walk away from the tax.

options_template.text: Whether the tax statute legally requires buyers or sellers to remit the tax to the government.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Statutory Incidence Fallacy): In the standard competitive model, statutory incidence does not alter the economic split of the tax burden.

options_template.text: The relative price elasticities of demand and supply, with the more inelastic side bearing the larger share.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Economic tax incidence depends on relative elasticities: the more inelastic side has fewer alternatives to escape the tax wedge and therefore absorbs the larger share.

options_template.text: A fixed 50/50 rule in which competitive markets always divide every per-unit tax equally between buyers and sellers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equal-Split Fallacy): A 50/50 split occurs only in the special case where $|\varepsilon_d| = \varepsilon_s$; otherwise the more inelastic side pays more.

options_template.text: The relative price elasticities of demand and supply, with the more elastic side bearing the larger share.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elasticity Incidence Reversal): The more elastic side can easily switch away or redirect production, shifting the bulk of the tax onto the more inelastic side.

questions.title: Comparing Quantity Responses Through a Common Initial Point
questions.prompt_template: Two linear demand curves—a steep curve $D_{\text{inelastic}}$ and a flatter curve $D_{\text{elastic}}$—intersect at the same initial point $E_1(Q_1 = 20,\; P_1 = \$60)$. If the market price drops from $\$60$ to $\$40$, what does the graph show?

hints.text: Start at $E_1(20, \$60)$ and trace horizontally across at $P_2 = \$40$ to see where each curve lands.
At a shared starting point $(Q_1, P_1)$, the flatter demand curve stretches further to the right for the same vertical drop in price.

options_template.text: Quantity demanded increases by more along the flatter curve $D_{\text{elastic}}$ than along the steeper curve $D_{\text{inelastic}}$.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Passing through the same initial point, a flatter demand curve yields a larger horizontal expansion in quantity demanded for the exact same price reduction.

options_template.text: Quantity demanded increases by more along the steeper curve $D_{\text{inelastic}}$ than along the flatter curve $D_{\text{elastic}}$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Steepness Reversal): A steeper demand curve has a smaller horizontal run per unit of vertical price drop, producing a smaller—not larger—quantity increase.

options_template.text: Both curves show the exact same increase in quantity demanded because both start at $E_1$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shared-Point Conflation): Sharing one intersection point means $Q_1$ and $P_1$ match initially, not that the curves respond identically once price moves away from $P_1$.

options_template.text: Both curves shift to the right because lower prices increase overall demand.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift vs. Movement Confusion): A change in the good's own price from $\$60$ to $\$40$ causes a movement along each demand curve, not a rightward shift of the curves.

questions.topic: Slope vs. Elasticity Along a Linear Demand Curve
questions.title: How Slope and Elasticity Change Moving Down a Linear Demand Curve
questions.prompt_template: As you move downward and to the right along a single downward-sloping straight-line demand curve, how do the curve's slope and its price elasticity magnitude $|\varepsilon_d|$ behave?

hints.text: Recall the Chapter 5 'Clear It Up' distinction between constant geometric slope and changing percentage bases.
Near the top-left, $P$ is high and $Q$ is low; near the bottom-right, $P$ is low and $Q$ is high.

options_template.text: Both the slope and $|\varepsilon_d|$ stay constant at every point on the line.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Elasticity Identity): A straight line has constant slope, but because $P/Q$ falls continuously moving down the line, $|\varepsilon_d|$ does not stay constant.

options_template.text: The slope becomes steeper while $|\varepsilon_d|$ increases continuously from bottom to top.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Nonlinear Slope Error): A straight-line demand curve has a single constant slope throughout—it does not grow steeper or flatter.

options_template.text: The slope remains constant, while $|\varepsilon_d|$ steadily decreases from elastic (above the midpoint) to unit elastic (at the midpoint) to inelastic (below the midpoint).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Along a linear demand curve, the slope is constant, whereas moving down-right lowers $P/Q$, causing $|\varepsilon_d|$ to fall from $>1$ to $1$ to $<1$.

options_template.text: The slope remains constant, while $|\varepsilon_d|$ steadily increases from inelastic at high prices to elastic at low prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Region Inversion): At high prices and low quantities, a $\$1$ change is a tiny $\%\Delta P$ and huge $\%\Delta Q$ (elastic); at low prices and high quantities, demand is inelastic.

questions.title: Graphical Shapes of Perfectly Inelastic and Perfectly Elastic Demand
questions.prompt_template: On a standard coordinate graph with Price ($P$) on the vertical axis and Quantity ($Q$) on the horizontal axis, what geometric shapes represent perfectly inelastic demand ($|\varepsilon_d| = 0$) and perfectly elastic demand ($|\varepsilon_d| = \infty$)?

hints.text: For perfectly inelastic demand, quantity $Q$ never changes even as price $P$ moves up or down.
Remember the visual mnemonic: a vertical line looks like the 'I' in Inelastic, while a horizontal line fixes price at one level.

options_template.text: Perfectly inelastic demand is a horizontal line, and perfectly elastic demand is a vertical line.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Axis-Orientation Swap): A horizontal line fixes $P$ while $Q$ varies infinitely (perfectly elastic); a vertical line fixes $Q$ while $P$ varies (perfectly inelastic).

options_template.text: Perfectly inelastic demand is a vertical line, and perfectly elastic demand is a horizontal line.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A vertical line holds $Q$ completely fixed at every price ($|\varepsilon_d| = 0$), whereas a horizontal line shows infinite quantity sensitivity at a single price ($|\varepsilon_d| = \infty$).

options_template.text: Perfectly inelastic demand is a 45-degree downward-sloping line, and perfectly elastic demand is a ray from the origin.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (45-Degree Misconception): A 45-degree downward line has constant slope $-1$, not zero elasticity, and an upward ray from the origin represents unit-elastic supply, not demand.

options_template.text: Both polar cases are downward-sloping curves that differ only in their vertical intercepts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept Confusion): Shifting a curve's vertical intercept does not produce the polar limits $|\varepsilon_d| = 0$ (vertical) or $|\varepsilon_d| = \infty$ (horizontal).

questions.title: Locating the Elastic Region of a Linear Demand Curve
questions.prompt_template: Consider the linear demand curve $P = 100 - 2Q$, which has a vertical price intercept of $\$100$ and a horizontal quantity intercept of $50$ units. Over which range of prices is demand elastic ($|\varepsilon_d| > 1$)?

hints.text: First locate the geometric midpoint of the straight line—halfway down the price intercept and halfway across the quantity intercept.
For any straight-line demand curve, the elastic region lies strictly above the unit-elastic midpoint price.

options_template.text: Strictly between $\$0$ and $\$50$ (corresponding to $25 < Q < 50$).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Lower-Half Reversal): Prices below the $\$50$ midpoint lie in the inelastic lower half where $|\varepsilon_d| < 1$.

options_template.text: Only at the exact price $P = \$50$ (corresponding to $Q = 25$).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Midpoint Misclassification): At the exact midpoint $(Q = 25, P = \$50)$, demand is unit elastic ($|\varepsilon_d| = 1$), not elastic.

options_template.text: Strictly between $\$50$ and $\$100$ (corresponding to $0 < Q < 25$).
options_template.feedback: Correct. The midpoint of $P = 100 - 2Q$ is $(Q = 25, P = \$50)$; every point above that midpoint ($\$50 < P < \$100$) lies in the elastic region where $|\varepsilon_d| > 1$.

options_template.text: At every price from $\$0$ to $\$100$, because the slope magnitude $|-2|$ exceeds $1$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Magnitude Trap): Comparing raw slope magnitude $|-2| > 1$ to $1$ mistakes slope for elasticity; elasticity varies from $\infty$ at $P=\$100$ down to $0$ at $P=\$0$.

questions.topic: Stacked Demand and Total Revenue Diagram
questions.title: Behavior of the Total Revenue Curve Past the Midpoint
questions.prompt_template: In a stacked diagram pairing linear demand $P = 100 - 2Q$ above its parabolic Total Revenue curve $TR(Q)$, what happens to Total Revenue as a seller lowers price enough to expand quantity sold beyond the midpoint $Q = 25$?

hints.text: Identify which elasticity region lies to the right of $Q = 25$ on the linear demand curve.
Once quantity moves past the peak of the $TR(Q)$ parabola, cutting price further puts the seller in the inelastic region.

options_template.text: Total Revenue continues to climb toward a maximum at $Q = 50$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Quantity-Maximization Fallacy): At $Q = 50$, price has fallen to $\$0$, so $TR = \$0$; revenue actually falls after $Q = 25$.

options_template.text: Total Revenue remains flat at $\$1{,}250$ for all quantities above $Q = 25$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Plateau Misconception): The $TR$ curve for linear demand is a downward-opening parabola with a single peak at $Q = 25$, not a flat plateau.

options_template.text: Total Revenue declines from its peak of $\$1{,}250$ toward $\$0$ because price cuts in the inelastic region lose more from the price effect than they gain from the quantity effect.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Past $Q = 25$, demand is inelastic ($|\varepsilon_d| < 1$); further price cuts reduce revenue per unit proportionally more than they increase quantity, pulling $TR$ downward.

options_template.text: Total Revenue becomes negative immediately after $Q = 25$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative-Revenue Confusion): While marginal revenue becomes negative past $Q = 25$, Total Revenue ($P \times Q$) remains positive everywhere between $Q = 0$ and $Q = 50$.

questions.title: Moving Along the Elastic Branch of the Total Revenue Curve
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a seller currently operates on the elastic upper half of a linear demand curve and reduces price modestly without crossing the unit-elastic midpoint. How is this price cut depicted on the corresponding $TR(Q)$ parabola?

hints.text: A price cut increases quantity sold $Q$, moving rightward along the horizontal axis.
On the left side of the $TR(Q)$ parabola (where demand is elastic), is the curve sloping upward or downward as $Q$ increases?

options_template.text: A movement upward and to the right along the rising left branch of the $TR$ parabola toward its peak.
options_template.feedback: Correct. In the elastic region, cutting price raises quantity enough that $TR$ climbs upward along the rising left side of the parabola toward the midpoint peak.

options_template.text: A movement downward and to the right along the falling right branch of the $TR$ parabola.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Branch): The falling right branch corresponds to the inelastic region below the midpoint, not the elastic upper half.

options_template.text: A movement downward and to the left toward the origin on the $TR$ parabola.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction of $Q$ Reversal): Cutting price increases quantity demanded ($Q \uparrow$), which moves rightward—not leftward—along the horizontal quantity axis.

options_template.text: An upward shift of the entire $TR$ parabola while quantity remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift vs. Movement Confusion): Changing price along a fixed demand curve causes a movement along the existing $TR(Q)$ curve, not a shift of the entire parabola.

questions.topic: Movements Along vs. Shifts of Demand
questions.title: Graphical Distinction Between Own-Price, Income, and Cross-Price Elasticities
questions.prompt_template: On a standard $(Q_x, P_x)$ market graph for Good $X$, how do own-price elasticity ($\varepsilon_d$), income elasticity ($\varepsilon_I$), and cross-price elasticity ($\varepsilon_{xy}$) differ geometrically?

hints.text: Ask which variable is plotted on the vertical axis ($P_x$) and which variables ($I$ and $P_y$) are held constant along a given demand curve.
Changes in $P_x$ move you along $D_x$; changes in $I$ or $P_y$ shift the entire curve $D_x$.

options_template.text: All three elasticities measure movements along a single stationary demand curve for Good $X$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (All-Movements Error): Only changes in $P_x$ cause movements along $D_x$; changes in income $I$ or a related good's price $P_y$ shift the entire curve.

options_template.text: All three elasticities measure shifts in the market supply curve rather than the demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Supply Confusion): $\varepsilon_d$, $\varepsilon_I$, and $\varepsilon_{xy}$ are all demand-side elasticities; supply responsiveness is captured by $\varepsilon_s$.

options_template.text: $\varepsilon_I$ and $\varepsilon_{xy}$ measure movements along the demand curve, whereas $\varepsilon_d$ measures vertical shifts of the demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-Movement Inversion): This swaps the geometric roles: own price $P_x$ is on the axis (movement along), while $I$ and $P_y$ are shift parameters.

options_template.text: $\varepsilon_d$ measures movement along a fixed demand curve for Good $X$, whereas $\varepsilon_I$ and $\varepsilon_{xy}$ measure horizontal shifts of the entire demand curve for Good $X$.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Own-price elasticity tracks responsiveness along a fixed demand curve, whereas income and cross-price elasticities quantify how far the demand curve shifts at a given $P_x$.

questions.title: Graphical Demand Shift for an Inferior Good When Income Rises
questions.prompt_template: Suppose household incomes rise across a metropolitan area, and instant ramen packs have a negative income elasticity of demand ($\varepsilon_I < 0$). Holding the price of ramen constant, how is this change illustrated in the market graph for instant ramen?

hints.text: A negative $\varepsilon_I$ identifies an inferior good: when income rises, do households buy more or less at every price?
A change in income shifts the entire demand curve rather than moving along it.

options_template.text: The demand curve for instant ramen shifts to the right.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Normal-Good Assumption): A rightward demand shift when income rises occurs for normal goods ($\varepsilon_I > 0$), not inferior goods ($\varepsilon_I < 0$).

options_template.text: Buyers move upward and to the left along a stationary demand curve for instant ramen.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement vs. Shift Error): Moving along a fixed demand curve occurs only when the price of ramen itself changes, not when consumer income changes.

options_template.text: The demand curve for instant ramen shifts to the left.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because $\varepsilon_I < 0$ indicates an inferior good, rising income reduces quantity demanded at every price, shifting the entire demand curve leftward.

options_template.text: The supply curve for instant ramen shifts to the left while demand stays unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Side of Market): Consumer income is a demand determinant; it shifts the demand curve rather than the supply curve.

questions.title: Demand Shift for Espresso Shots When Oat Milk Price Rises
questions.prompt_template: Suppose local café espresso shots ($X$) and oat milk ($Y$) have a cross-price elasticity of $\varepsilon_{xy} = -0.47$. If the price of oat milk rises significantly, what happens on the $(Q_x, P_x)$ diagram for espresso shots?

hints.text: Use the negative sign of $\varepsilon_{xy}$ to determine whether espresso shots and oat milk are complements or substitutes.
When a complement becomes more expensive, consumers buy less of both goods at every price of $X$.

options_template.text: The demand curve for espresso shots shifts to the left.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because $\varepsilon_{xy} < 0$ identifies complements, a higher price for oat milk reduces demand for espresso shots at every price, shifting $D_{\text{espresso}}$ leftward.

options_template.text: The demand curve for espresso shots shifts to the right.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Complement-Substitute Swap): A rightward shift of $D_x$ when $P_y$ rises occurs for substitutes ($\varepsilon_{xy} > 0$), not complements ($\varepsilon_{xy} < 0$).

options_template.text: Consumers move downward along a stationary demand curve for espresso shots.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement vs. Shift Error): Because the price of a related good ($P_y$) changed rather than the price of espresso ($P_x$), the entire espresso demand curve shifts.

options_template.text: The demand curve for espresso shots becomes completely vertical.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift vs. Slope-Rotation Confusion): A related-good price change shifts the demand curve horizontally; it does not transform demand into a perfectly inelastic vertical line.

questions.title: Demand Shift for Commuter Rail When Downtown Parking Prices Rise
questions.prompt_template: Suppose downtown garage parking ($Y$) and commuter rail ($X$) are substitutes ($\varepsilon_{xy} > 0$). If municipal downtown parking rates rise sharply, what graphical change occurs in the commuter rail market?

hints.text: With $\varepsilon_{xy} > 0$, rising prices for Good $Y$ push commuters toward Good $X$.
An increase in demand at every rail fare is represented by shifting the demand curve in which direction?

options_template.text: The demand curve for commuter rail shifts to the left, lowering ridership.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Substitute-Complement Swap): A leftward shift would happen if parking and rail were complements ($\varepsilon_{xy} < 0$), not substitutes ($\varepsilon_{xy} > 0$).

options_template.text: The demand curve for commuter rail shifts to the right, increasing ridership at any given fare.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because $\varepsilon_{xy} > 0$ means the two services are substitutes, pricier downtown parking drives commuters onto rail, shifting the rail demand curve rightward.

options_template.text: Commuters move downward and to the right along a fixed commuter rail demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Own-Price vs. Cross-Price Confusion): A movement along the rail demand curve requires a change in rail fares themselves, whereas a change in parking prices shifts the rail demand curve.

options_template.text: The supply curve for commuter rail shifts immediately to the right.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Supply Confusion): Higher parking rates alter commuter demand for rail travel rather than automatically adding rail cars to supply.

questions.title: Price and Quantity Adjustments Following a Demand Surge Across Time Horizons
questions.prompt_template: Starting from a common initial equilibrium $E_1$, demand surges from $D_1$ to $D_2$. Compare the resulting equilibrium prices across three supply curves passing through $E_1$: vertical immediate-run supply ($S_{\text{immediate}}$), steep short-run supply ($S_{\text{short-run}}$), and flat long-run supply ($S_{\text{long-run}}$).

hints.text: Trace where $D_2$ intersects each of the three supply curves (as in Figure 5.3 of the chapter).
The more vertical the supply curve, the less quantity can expand and the higher price must climb to clear the market.

options_template.text: $P_{\text{lr}} > P_{\text{sr}} > P_{\text{imm}}$, because long-run entry drives prices progressively higher.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Time-Horizon Reversal): Long-run factory expansion and entry flatten the supply curve, allowing larger quantity growth and moderating—not amplifying—the price increase.

options_template.text: $P_{\text{imm}} = P_{\text{sr}} = P_{\text{lr}}$, because all three supply curves pass through the same initial point $E_1$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Initial-Equilibrium Fixation): Sharing the pre-surge equilibrium $E_1$ does not mean all three curves intersect the shifted demand curve $D_2$ at the same price.

options_template.text: $P_{\text{imm}} > P_{\text{sr}} > P_{\text{lr}}$, while equilibrium quantity expands most in the long run ($Q_{\text{lr}} > Q_{\text{sr}} > Q_1$).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Fixed immediate supply ($\varepsilon_s = 0$) forces price to spike highest to $P_{\text{imm}}$ with zero output gain; as supply flattens over the short and long run, quantity rises and price moderates.

options_template.text: $P_{\text{sr}} > P_{\text{imm}} > P_{\text{lr}}$, because output shrinks in the immediate run before expanding.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Output-Contraction Error): Along vertical $S_{\text{immediate}}$, quantity stays fixed at $Q_1$ (it does not shrink), and its vertical slope produces the highest—not middle—price spike.

questions.title: Visual Tax Burden When Demand Is Steep and Supply Is Flat
questions.prompt_template: At the pre-tax equilibrium $E^*(Q^*, P^*)$ of a competitive market, the demand curve is very steep (inelastic) and the supply curve is relatively flat (elastic). When a per-unit excise tax $t = P_b - P_s$ is introduced, how do the shaded buyer and seller tax-burden rectangles compare graphically?

hints.text: Compare the vertical distance $P_b - P^*$ (buyer burden per unit) with $P^* - P_s$ (seller burden per unit) at the post-tax quantity $Q_t$.
With steep demand and flat supply, the tax wedge pushes $P_b$ far above $P^*$ while $P_s$ dips only slightly below $P^*$.

options_template.text: The seller burden rectangle $(P^* - P_s) \times Q_t$ is vertically much taller than the buyer burden rectangle $(P_b - P^*) \times Q_t$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Incidence Graph Reversal): A taller seller rectangle occurs when supply is steep (inelastic) and demand is flat (elastic), not when demand is steep and supply is flat.

options_template.text: Post-tax quantity $Q_t$ exceeds pre-tax quantity $Q^*$ because the tax wedge widens the market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Quantity-Expansion Error): A per-unit excise tax drives a wedge between buyer price and seller net price that shrinks quantity traded ($Q_t < Q^*$), unless one curve is perfectly inelastic.

options_template.text: Both rectangles have identical height because the vertical tax wedge $t$ is always bisected at $P^*$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Midpoint Wedge Assumption): $P^*$ bisects the tax wedge $P_b - P_s$ only when demand and supply have equal elasticity magnitudes at equilibrium.

options_template.text: The buyer burden rectangle $(P_b - P^*) \times Q_t$ is vertically much taller than the seller burden rectangle $(P^* - P_s) \times Q_t$.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When demand is relatively inelastic and supply is relatively elastic at $E^*$, sellers pass most of the tax forward, making $P_b - P^* > P^* - P_s$.

questions.title: Graphical Effects of an Excise Tax with Perfectly Inelastic Supply
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a competitive market has a completely vertical supply curve ($\varepsilon_s = 0$) and a standard downward-sloping demand curve. If the government imposes a per-unit excise tax $t$, what happens graphically to equilibrium quantity $Q_t$, buyer price $P_b$, and seller net price $P_s$?

hints.text: Remember that along a vertical supply curve, quantity supplied is fixed at $Q^*$ no matter what net price sellers receive.
At quantity $Q^*$, the demand curve pins down the maximum price buyers are willing to pay ($P_b = P^*$).

options_template.text: $Q_t < Q^*$, $P_b = P^* + t$, and $P_s = P^*$, so buyers bear $100\%$ of the tax.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Vertical-Demand Swap): Buyers pay $100\%$ of the tax with unchanged quantity when demand is vertical ($|\varepsilon_d| = 0$), not when supply is vertical ($\varepsilon_s = 0$).

options_template.text: $Q_t = Q^*$, $P_b = P^*$, and $P_s = P^* - t$, so sellers absorb $100\%$ of the tax burden.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because vertical supply fixes quantity at $Q^*$, buyers still pay the demand price $P^*$ at $Q^*$, forcing sellers' net price down by the full tax ($P_s = P^* - t$).

options_template.text: $Q_t < Q^*$, and the tax is split equally so $P_b = P^* + t/2$ and $P_s = P^* - t/2$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equal-Split Fallacy): With vertical supply, quantity does not drop and sellers have zero ability to escape the tax through output reduction.

options_template.text: $Q_t = 0$, because sellers shut down immediately whenever a tax is levied on a vertical supply curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shutdown Confusion): A vertical supply curve indicates fixed quantity supplied across the relevant positive net prices ($P_s > 0$), not immediate exit to zero output.

questions.title: Computing Midpoint Elasticity of Demand (Elastic Interval)
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a boutique bakery lowers the price of its specialty gift box from $P_1 = \$10$ to $P_2 = \$6$, and daily sales increase from $Q_1 = 5$ to $Q_2 = 15$ boxes. Using the midpoint formula, what is the absolute price elasticity of demand $|\varepsilon_d|$ over this price range?

hints.text: Compute the midpoint percentage changes separately: $\%\Delta Q_d = (Q_2 - Q_1)/[(Q_1 + Q_2)/2]$ and $\%\Delta P = (P_2 - P_1)/[(P_1 + P_2)/2]$.
Here $Q_{\text{mid}} = 10$ giving $\%\Delta Q_d = +10/10 = +1.00$, and $P_{\text{mid}} = \$8$ giving $\%\Delta P = -4/8 = -0.50$. Now divide $|\%\Delta Q_d / \%\Delta P|$.

options_template.text: $0.50$ (inelastic)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Elasticity Ratio): Dividing $|\%\Delta P|$ by $|\%\Delta Q_d|$ ($0.50 / 1.00 = 0.50$) flips the elasticity formula upside down.

options_template.text: $2.00$ (elastic)
$2.50$ (elastic)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Raw Slope Substitution): Computing $|\Delta Q / \Delta P| = 10 / 4 = 2.50$ uses the raw slope rather than percentage changes.

options_template.text: $5.00$ (elastic)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Initial-Value Base Error): Using $Q_1 = 5$ ($10/5 = 2.00$) and $P_1 = \$10$ ($-4/10 = -0.40$) instead of midpoint averages yields $2.00 / 0.40 = 5.00$, which suffers from direction bias.

questions.title: Computing Midpoint Elasticity of Demand (Inelastic Interval)
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a regional ferry operator raises its commuter ticket price from $P_1 = \$16$ to $P_2 = \$24$, and daily ticket sales fall from $Q_1 = 110$ to $Q_2 = 90$ tickets. Using the midpoint formula, what is the absolute price elasticity of demand $|\varepsilon_d|$?

hints.text: Find both midpoints first: $Q_{\text{mid}} = (110 + 90)/2$ and $P_{\text{mid}} = (16 + 24)/2$.
With $Q_{\text{mid}} = 100$ and $P_{\text{mid}} = \$20$, we get $\%\Delta Q_d = -20/100 = -0.20$ and $\%\Delta P = +8/20 = +0.40$.

options_template.text: $0.40$ (inelastic)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inconsistent Base / Inverse-Slope Error): Using the initial price $P_1 = \$16$ ($8/16 = 0.50$) instead of $P_{\text{mid}} = \$20$ gives $0.20 / 0.50 = 0.40$ (which also equals raw $|\Delta P / \Delta Q| = 8/20$).

options_template.text: $2.00$ (elastic)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Elasticity Ratio): Computing $|\%\Delta P / \%\Delta Q_d| = 0.40 / 0.20 = 2.00$ inverts the numerator and denominator.

options_template.text: $0.50$ (inelastic)
$2.50$ (elastic)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Raw Slope Substitution): Computing $|\Delta Q / \Delta P| = 20 / 8 = 2.50$ reports the raw slope instead of the ratio of percentage changes.

questions.title: Calculating Point Elasticity Along a Linear Demand Function
questions.prompt_template: Consider the stylized linear demand function $Q_d = 120 - 4P$. Using the point elasticity formula $\varepsilon_d = \frac{dQ_d}{dP} \cdot \frac{P}{Q_d}$, what is the absolute point price elasticity of demand $|\varepsilon_d|$ at $P = \$20$?

hints.text: First substitute $P = 20$ into $Q_d = 120 - 4P$ to find the corresponding quantity $Q_d$.
Identify the derivative $dQ_d/dP = -4$, then multiply $|-4|$ by the ratio $P/Q_d = 20/40$.

options_template.text: $2.00$ (elastic)
options_template.feedback: Correct. At $P = \$20$, $Q_d = 120 - 4(20) = 40$ and $dQ_d/dP = -4$, giving $|\varepsilon_d| = |-4 \times (20/40)| = 2.00$ (elastic).

options_template.text: $4.00$ (elastic)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Elasticity Conflation): Reporting $|dQ_d/dP| = 4.00$ stops at the derivative and forgets to multiply by $P/Q_d = 20/40$.

options_template.text: $0.50$ (inelastic)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Slope Factor): Computing only $P/Q_d = 20/40 = 0.50$ omits the slope factor $|dQ_d/dP| = 4$.

options_template.text: $0.125$ (inelastic)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Derivative Error): Using $|dP/dQ_d| = 1/4 = 0.25$ instead of $|dQ_d/dP| = 4$ gives $0.25 \times (20/40) = 0.125$.

questions.title: Computing Total Revenue Change and Classifying Elasticity
questions.prompt_template: A stylized regional theater reduces its matinee ticket price from $P_1 = \$40$ to $P_2 = \$30$, and ticket sales rise from $Q_1 = 200$ to $Q_2 = 300$ per show. What is the change in Total Revenue ($\Delta TR = TR_2 - TR_1$), and what does the Total Revenue Test conclude about demand over this interval?

hints.text: Calculate initial revenue $TR_1 = P_1 \times Q_1$ and new revenue $TR_2 = P_2 \times Q_2$, then find $TR_2 - TR_1$.
Compare the direction of the price change ($P \downarrow$) with the direction of the revenue change ($TR \uparrow$ or $TR \downarrow$).

options_template.text: $\Delta TR = +\$1{,}000$; demand is inelastic over this interval.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Increase-Means-Inelastic Fallacy): Rising revenue indicates inelastic demand only when price rises; when price falls and $TR$ rises (opposite directions), demand is elastic.

options_template.text: $\Delta TR = -\$1{,}000$; demand is inelastic over this interval.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal in $\Delta TR$): Subtracting $TR_1 - TR_2 = \$8{,}000 - \$9{,}000 = -\$1{,}000$ reverses the change; revenue actually increased by $\$1{,}000$.

options_template.text: $\Delta TR = +\$3{,}000$; demand is elastic over this interval.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Price Effect): Multiplying the extra $100$ tickets by $\$30$ counts only the $+\$3{,}000$ quantity effect while ignoring the $-\$2{,}000$ price loss on the original $200$ tickets.

options_template.text: $\Delta TR = +\$1{,}000$; demand is elastic over this interval.
options_template.feedback: Correct. $TR_1 = \$40 \times 200 = \$8{,}000$ and $TR_2 = \$30 \times 300 = \$9{,}000$, so $\Delta TR = +\$1{,}000$. Because price fell while $TR$ rose (opposite directions), demand is elastic ($|\varepsilon_d| = 1.40 > 1$).

questions.title: Finding the Revenue-Maximizing Price and Maximum Total Revenue
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a campus bike-rental shop faces the stylized linear demand schedule $P = 80 - 2Q$, where $P$ is the rental price in dollars and $Q$ is daily rentals. At the unit-elastic midpoint, what price $P$ maximizes Total Revenue, and what is the maximum daily Total Revenue ($TR_{\max}$)?

hints.text: Find the vertical price intercept (at $Q = 0$) and horizontal quantity intercept (at $P = 0$) of $P = 80 - 2Q$.
For a linear demand curve, the unit-elastic midpoint occurs at half the vertical intercept and half the horizontal intercept; multiply those two values to get $TR_{\max}$.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept-Midpoint Swap): Setting $P = \$20$ (half the horizontal intercept $40$ instead of half the vertical intercept $80$) yields $Q = 30$ and $TR = \$600$ in the inelastic region.
Diagnostic fallacy (Full-Intercept Quantity Error): Multiplying midpoint price $\$40$ by the full horizontal intercept $Q = 40$ instead of midpoint quantity $Q = 20$ doubles true maximum revenue.
Diagnostic fallacy (High-Price Fallacy): Charging $P = \$60$ places the shop in the elastic region ($Q = 10$, $TR = \$600$), leaving $\$200$ of revenue on the table compared to the midpoint.
Correct. The intercepts are $P_{\max} = \$80$ and $Q_{\max} = 40$, so the unit-elastic midpoint is $P = \$40$ and $Q = 20$, maximizing Total Revenue at $TR_{\max} = \$40 \times 20 = \$800$.

questions.topic: Linking Midpoint Elasticity and Total Revenue
questions.title: Verifying the Total Revenue Test with the Midpoint Formula
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a stylized digital magazine raises its monthly subscription price from $P_1 = \$12$ to $P_2 = \$18$, and paid subscribers fall from $Q_1 = 550$ to $Q_2 = 450$. What are the midpoint price elasticity $|\varepsilon_d|$ and the change in monthly Total Revenue ($\Delta TR = TR_2 - TR_1$)?

hints.text: Compute $TR_1 = 12 \times 550$ and $TR_2 = 18 \times 450$ first to predict whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
Verify with the midpoint formula: $Q_{\text{mid}} = 500$ ($\%\Delta Q_d = -100/500 = -0.20$) and $P_{\text{mid}} = \$15$ ($\%\Delta P = +6/15 = +0.40$).

options_template.text: $|\varepsilon_d| = 2.00$ and $\Delta TR = +\$1{,}500$
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Ratio Contradicting TR Test): Dividing $0.40 / 0.20 = 2.00$ inverts the formula and contradicts the Total Revenue Test—if $|\varepsilon_d|$ were $2.00$, raising price would reduce $TR$.

options_template.text: $|\varepsilon_d| = 0.50$ and $\Delta TR = -\$1{,}500$
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed $\Delta TR$ Subtraction): Computing $TR_1 - TR_2 = \$6{,}600 - \$8{,}100 = -\$1{,}500$ flips the sign; revenue increased by $+\$1{,}500$.

options_template.text: $|\varepsilon_d| = 0.50$ and $\Delta TR = +\$1{,}500$
options_template.feedback: Correct. $\%\Delta Q_d = -0.20$ and $\%\Delta P = +0.40$ yield $|\varepsilon_d| = 0.50$ (inelastic), matching $TR_2 - TR_1 = \$8{,}100 - \$6{,}600 = +\$1{,}500$.

options_template.text: $|\varepsilon_d| = 0.40$ and $\Delta TR = +\$3{,}300$
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Initial-Price Base & Omitted Quantity Loss): Using $P_1 = \$12$ gives $\%\Delta P = 0.50$ and $0.20/0.50 = 0.40$, while $+\$3{,}300$ ($\$6 \times 550$) ignores the revenue lost from $100$ departing subscribers.

questions.title: Calculating and Classifying Income Elasticity via the Midpoint Formula
questions.prompt_template: In a hypothetical household panel, average annual income rises from $I_1 = \$40{,}000$ to $I_2 = \$60{,}000$, and annual fine-dining outings increase from $Q_1 = 20$ to $Q_2 = 60$ per year (holding prices constant). Using the midpoint formula, what is the income elasticity of demand ($\varepsilon_I$) and how are fine-dining outings classified?

hints.text: Compute $\%\Delta Q_d$ and $\%\Delta I$ using midpoint averages: $Q_{\text{mid}} = 40$ and $I_{\text{mid}} = \$50{,}000$.
Keep the algebraic sign of $\varepsilon_I = \%\Delta Q_d / \%\Delta I$: positive above $1$ is a normal luxury, between $0$ and $1$ is a normal necessity, and negative is inferior.

options_template.text: $\varepsilon_I = +0.40$ (normal necessity)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Income Elasticity Ratio): Computing $\%\Delta I / \%\Delta Q_d = 0.40 / 1.00 = +0.40$ flips the numerator and denominator and misclassifies the good as a necessity.

options_template.text: $\varepsilon_I = -2.50$ (inferior good)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Spurious Negative Sign): Both income and quantity increased, so $\varepsilon_I$ is positive; attaching a negative sign confuses income elasticity with own-price elasticity.

options_template.text: $\varepsilon_I = +4.00$ (normal luxury)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Initial-Value Base Error): Using $Q_1 = 20$ ($40/20 = 2.00$) and $I_1 = \$40{,}000$ ($20{,}000/40{,}000 = 0.50$) instead of midpoint averages gives $2.00 / 0.50 = +4.00$.

options_template.text: $\varepsilon_I = +2.50$ (normal luxury)
options_template.feedback: Correct. $\%\Delta Q_d = (60 - 20)/40 = +1.00$ and $\%\Delta I = 20{,}000 / 50{,}000 = +0.40$, so $\varepsilon_I = +1.00 / +0.40 = +2.50 > 1$, classifying fine-dining outings as a normal luxury.

questions.title: Computing Cross-Price Elasticity and Identifying Related Goods
questions.prompt_template: Suppose the price of wireless studio headphones (Good $Y$) increases from $P_{y1} = \$40$ to $P_{y2} = \$60$, and weekly local sales of carrying cases sized for those headphones (Good $X$) decline from $Q_{x1} = 110$ to $Q_{x2} = 90$ units. Using the midpoint formula, what is $\varepsilon_{xy}$ and how are the two goods related?

hints.text: Compute $\%\Delta Q_x = (90 - 110)/100$ and $\%\Delta P_y = (60 - 40)/50$, keeping both signs.
Never take the absolute value for $\varepsilon_{xy}$: negative indicates complements, while positive indicates substitutes.

options_template.text: $\varepsilon_{xy} = -0.50$ (complements)
options_template.feedback: Correct. $\%\Delta Q_x = -20/100 = -0.20$ and $\%\Delta P_y = +20/50 = +0.40$, giving $\varepsilon_{xy} = -0.20 / +0.40 = -0.50 < 0$, which confirms the two goods are complements.

options_template.text: $\varepsilon_{xy} = +0.50$ (substitutes)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dropped Algebraic Sign): Taking the absolute value erases the negative sign and falsely classifies complementary goods as substitutes.

options_template.text: $\varepsilon_{xy} = -2.00$ (complements)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Cross-Price Ratio): Dividing $\%\Delta P_y / \%\Delta Q_x = +0.40 / (-0.20) = -2.00$ puts price in the numerator and quantity in the denominator.

options_template.text: $\varepsilon_{xy} = +2.00$ (substitutes)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double Error: Inverted Ratio & Dropped Sign): Dividing $|\%\Delta P_y / \%\Delta Q_x| = 0.40 / 0.20 = +2.00$ both flips the ratio and drops the negative sign.

questions.title: Computing Midpoint Price Elasticity of Supply
questions.prompt_template: When the market price of artisanal coffee beans rises from $P_1 = \$15$ to $P_2 = \$25$ per pound, monthly quantity supplied expands from $Q_{s1} = 400$ to $Q_{s2} = 600$ pounds. Using the midpoint formula, what is the price elasticity of supply ($\varepsilon_s$) over this interval?

hints.text: Calculate the midpoint averages first: $Q_{s,\text{mid}} = (400 + 600)/2 = 500$ and $P_{\text{mid}} = (15 + 25)/2 = \$20$.
Divide $\%\Delta Q_s = +200/500 = +0.40$ by $\%\Delta P = +10/20 = +0.50$ and compare the result to $1$.

options_template.text: $1.25$ (elastic supply)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Supply Ratio): Dividing $\%\Delta P / \%\Delta Q_s = 0.50 / 0.40 = 1.25$ flips the elasticity formula upside down.

options_template.text: $0.80$ (inelastic supply)
options_template.feedback: Correct. $\%\Delta Q_s = 200/500 = +0.40$ and $\%\Delta P = 10/20 = +0.50$, yielding $\varepsilon_s = 0.40 / 0.50 = 0.80 < 1$ (inelastic supply).

options_template.text: $0.75$ (inelastic supply)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Initial-Value Base Error): Computing $(200/400) / (10/15) = 0.50 / (2/3) = 0.75$ uses initial values instead of midpoint averages.

options_template.text: $20.0$ (elastic supply)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Raw Slope Substitution): Computing $\Delta Q_s / \Delta P = 200 / 10 = 20.0$ reports the raw slope instead of the unit-free ratio of percentage changes.

questions.title: Calculating Point Supply Elasticity from a Linear Supply Function
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a stylized producer faces the linear supply function $Q_s = -30 + 5P$. Using the point supply elasticity formula $\varepsilon_s = \frac{dQ_s}{dP} \cdot \frac{P}{Q_s}$, what is $\varepsilon_s$ at $P = \$16$?

hints.text: First plug $P = 16$ into $Q_s = -30 + 5P$ to obtain $Q_s$.
With $dQ_s/dP = 5$ and $Q_s = 50$, evaluate $5 \times (16 / 50)$.

options_template.text: $0.32$ (inelastic supply)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Slope Factor): Calculating $P / Q_s = 16 / 50 = 0.32$ forgets to multiply by the derivative $dQ_s / dP = 5$.

options_template.text: $0.625$ (inelastic supply)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Point Formula): Evaluating $(dP/dQ_s) \cdot (Q_s/P) = (1/5) \times (50/16) = 0.625$ computes $1/\varepsilon_s$ instead of $\varepsilon_s$.

options_template.text: $1.60$ (elastic supply)
options_template.feedback: Correct. At $P = \$16$, $Q_s = -30 + 5(16) = 50$, so $\varepsilon_s = 5 \times (16 / 50) = 80 / 50 = 1.60 > 1$ (elastic supply).

options_template.text: $5.00$ (elastic supply)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Elasticity Conflation): Reporting $dQ_s/dP = 5.00$ mistakes the linear supply coefficient for the point elasticity.

questions.title: Solving for Post-Tax Buyer Burden in a Linear Competitive Market
questions.prompt_template: Consider a stylized competitive market with linear demand $P_d = 90 - 3Q$ and linear supply $P_s = 10 + Q$. Suppose the government levies a per-unit excise tax of $t = \$16$. What are the buyer's dollar tax burden per unit ($P_b - P^*$) and percentage share of the tax?

hints.text: First solve $90 - 3Q = 10 + Q$ for the pre-tax equilibrium $(Q^*, P^*)$, then solve the tax wedge $(90 - 3Q_t) - (10 + Q_t) = 16$ for $Q_t$.
With $Q^* = 20, P^* = \$30$ and $Q_t = 16$, plug $Q_t = 16$ into $P_d = 90 - 3Q_t$ to find $P_b$, then compute $(P_b - P^*)$ and $(P_b - P^*)/16$.

options_template.text: $\$4$ per unit ($25\%$ of the tax)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Buyer-Seller Burden Swap): $\$4$ per unit ($P^* - P_s = \$30 - \$26$, or $25\%$) is the seller's burden, not the buyer's burden.

options_template.text: $\$8$ per unit ($50\%$ of the tax)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equal-Split Assumption): Assuming the $\$16$ tax splits 50/50 ignores that demand ($|\varepsilon_d| = 0.50$) is more inelastic than supply ($\varepsilon_s = 1.50$) at equilibrium.

options_template.text: $\$16$ per unit ($100\%$ of the tax)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Full Pass-Through Assumption): Buyers would pay the entire $\$16$ tax only if demand were perfectly inelastic ($|\varepsilon_d| = 0$) or supply were perfectly elastic ($\varepsilon_s = \infty$).

options_template.text: $\$12$ per unit ($75\%$ of the tax)
options_template.feedback: Correct. Pre-tax equilibrium is $Q^* = 20, P^* = \$30$. The tax wedge gives $80 - 4Q_t = 16 \Rightarrow Q_t = 16$, so $P_b = 90 - 3(16) = \$42$ and buyer burden is $\$42 - \$30 = \$12$ ($12/16 = 75\%$).

questions.title: Computing Seller Tax Share via the Elasticity Pass-Through Formula
questions.prompt_template: At the pre-tax equilibrium of a stylized market for local marina slips, the absolute price elasticity of demand is $|\varepsilon_d| = 1.60$ and the price elasticity of supply is $\varepsilon_s = 0.40$. Using the elasticity pass-through formula for a small per-unit excise tax of $t = \$20$, what are the seller's percentage share and dollar tax burden per unit?

hints.text: Recall the pass-through shares: Buyer Share $= \varepsilon_s / (\varepsilon_s + |\varepsilon_d|)$ and Seller Share $= |\varepsilon_d| / (\varepsilon_s + |\varepsilon_d|)$.
Because supply is much more inelastic ($0.40$) than demand ($1.60$), sellers must bear the larger share: compute $1.60 / (0.40 + 1.60)$ and multiply by $\$20$.

options_template.text: $80\%$ of the tax ($\$16$ per unit)
options_template.feedback: Correct. Seller Share $= |\varepsilon_d| / (\varepsilon_s + |\varepsilon_d|) = 1.60 / (0.40 + 1.60) = 0.80$ ($80\%$), so sellers absorb $0.80 \times \$20 = \$16$ per unit.

options_template.text: $20\%$ of the tax ($\$4$ per unit)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Numerator Swap): Computing $\varepsilon_s / (\varepsilon_s + |\varepsilon_d|) = 0.40 / 2.00 = 20\%$ ($\$4$) gives the buyer's share rather than the seller's share.

options_template.text: $50\%$ of the tax ($\$10$ per unit)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equal-Split Fallacy): An equal split occurs only when $|\varepsilon_d| = \varepsilon_s$; here supply is four times more inelastic than demand.

options_template.text: $100\%$ of the tax ($\$20$ per unit)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inelastic vs. Perfectly Inelastic Confusion): Having inelastic supply ($\varepsilon_s = 0.40 < 1$) means sellers bear most—not all—of the tax; $100\%$ burden requires $\varepsilon_s = 0$.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Designing Peak vs. Off-Peak Transit Fares to Close a Budget Gap
questions.prompt_template: A metropolitan transit authority faces a budget shortfall. Stylized ridership analysis indicates that rush-hour commuter rail demand is inelastic ($|\varepsilon_d| < 1$), whereas weekend leisure rail demand is elastic ($|\varepsilon_d| > 1$). To increase total farebox revenue from BOTH rider groups simultaneously, what fare strategy should the authority adopt?

hints.text: Apply the Total Revenue Test separately to each group: how should price move to raise $TR$ when demand is inelastic versus elastic?
For inelastic rush-hour commuters, price and revenue move together; for elastic weekend riders, price and revenue move in opposite directions.

options_template.text: Raise fares for both rush-hour commuters and weekend leisure riders.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uniform Price-Hike Fallacy): Raising fares on elastic weekend riders causes ridership to fall more than proportionally, reducing weekend farebox revenue.

options_template.text: Raise rush-hour peak fares and lower weekend off-peak fares.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Raising inelastic peak fares increases revenue (price effect dominates), while lowering elastic off-peak fares attracts enough additional riders to raise revenue (quantity effect dominates).

options_template.text: Lower rush-hour peak fares and raise weekend off-peak fares.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Pricing Strategy): Cutting inelastic peak fares lowers revenue, and raising elastic off-peak fares also lowers revenue—worsening the deficit on both fronts.

options_template.text: Lower fares for both groups to maximize total ridership.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ridership-Revenue Conflation): Lowering fares on inelastic peak commuters expands ridership only slightly while cutting revenue per ticket, reducing peak farebox revenue.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Avoiding Over-Extrapolation from a Midpoint Elasticity Estimate
questions.prompt_template: A municipal transit report finds a midpoint price elasticity of $|\varepsilon_d| = 1.80$ after raising a monthly express pass from $\$80$ to $\$100$. A commentator then asserts that 'every $1\%$ fare increase at any price level will cut ridership by exactly $1.80\%$.' Why is this assertion analytically flawed?

hints.text: Recall what Chapter 5 emphasizes about midpoint (arc) elasticity versus point elasticity along a demand curve.
Think about whether elasticity stays constant across all price ranges along a typical linear or general demand curve.

options_template.text: Because an arc elasticity measures average responsiveness over a specific price interval ($\$80$–$\$100$), and elasticity generally varies across different price and quantity levels.
options_template.feedback: Correct. As Chapter 5 notes, a midpoint arc estimate applies only to the measured price interval and is not a universal forecast for every $1\%$ price change at other price levels.

options_template.text: Because $|\varepsilon_d| = 1.80$ means ridership actually rises by $1.80\%$ whenever fares increase by $1\%$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dropped Law of Demand): Taking the absolute value reports magnitude, not a positive relationship; higher fares reduce quantity demanded.

options_template.text: Because the midpoint formula is valid only when demand is inelastic ($|\varepsilon_d| < 1$).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Formula Domain Myth): The midpoint formula applies equally to elastic, unit-elastic, and inelastic intervals.

options_template.text: Because price elasticity of demand can never exceed $1.00$ for public transit services.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Arbitrary Bound Error): Demand elasticity can take any nonnegative value; express transit passes with driving or carpool alternatives can readily have $|\varepsilon_d| > 1$ over a high price interval.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Short-Run vs. Long-Run Consumer Adjustment to Fuel Prices
questions.prompt_template: When retail gasoline prices jump unexpectedly, households typically cut fuel consumption far less during the first month than they do if high prices persist for five years. Which economic mechanism best explains this difference?

hints.text: Consider what choices are locked in during a single month versus what adjustments become feasible over several years.
Connect household flexibility over time to the fourth structural determinant of price elasticity of demand.

options_template.text: Gasoline becomes an inferior good after five years, causing the demand curve to slope upward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Income vs. Own-Price Confusion): Time-horizon adjustment reflects increasing own-price elasticity through substitution, not an upward-sloping demand curve or inferior-good status.

options_template.text: Gasoline takes up a smaller share of the household budget after five years of high prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Budget-Share Mechanism Error): Higher sustained prices do not shrink gasoline's budget share on their own; rather, households actively adopt substitutes over time.

options_template.text: The Law of Demand holds only in the long run and does not apply during the first month after a price change.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Short-Run Law-of-Demand Denial): Consumers still reduce quantity demanded in the short run (just by a smaller percentage), so the Law of Demand holds in both horizons.

options_template.text: Over a longer time horizon, buyers have more opportunities to substitute—such as buying fuel-efficient vehicles, switching to transit, or relocating closer to work—making demand more elastic.
options_template.feedback: Correct. In the short run, drivers are locked into existing cars and commute patterns; over longer horizons, expanded substitution choices increase price elasticity of demand.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Narrow Brand Demand vs. Broad Category Demand
questions.prompt_template: Why is the price elasticity of demand for a single brand of bottled sparkling water typically much higher than the price elasticity of demand for all drinking beverages combined?

hints.text: Compare how easy it is to replace one brand of sparkling water versus replacing all beverages altogether.
Connect narrow vs. broad market definitions directly to the availability of close substitutes.

options_template.text: All drinking beverages combined take up a smaller share of household income than a single brand of sparkling water.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Budget-Share Inversion): A broad category (all beverages) takes up a larger—not smaller—share of household budgets than a single brand within it.

options_template.text: A single brand of sparkling water has many close substitutes (other brands and tap water), whereas the broad category of all drinking beverages has virtually no substitutes.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Narrowly defined goods face abundant close substitutes, making buyers highly price-sensitive; broadly defined necessities have few substitutes and far more inelastic demand.

options_template.text: Broad product categories always have flatter demand curves because they include more consumers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope vs. Elasticity & Market-Size Fallacy): Aggregating more consumers scales quantity horizontally without making percentage responsiveness higher; fewer substitutes make broad categories less elastic.

options_template.text: Producers of sparkling water have perfectly inelastic supply, which forces demand to be elastic.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Determines-Demand Fallacy): Supply elasticity does not determine consumer demand elasticity; availability of buyer substitutes drives demand elasticity.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Total Revenue Maximization vs. Profit Maximization
questions.title: Why Maximizing Total Revenue Differs from Maximizing Profit
questions.prompt_template: A campus bookstore manager sets hoodie prices at the exact unit-elastic midpoint ($|\varepsilon_d| = 1$) of a linear demand curve to maximize Total Revenue. If each hoodie costs the bookstore $\$20$ wholesale to purchase (positive marginal cost), why does this midpoint price fail to maximize profit?

hints.text: Recall the Chapter 5 caveat that the midpoint maximizes Total Revenue 'before accounting for production costs.'
Near the top of the $TR(Q)$ parabola, raising price slightly barely changes Total Revenue while selling fewer hoodies saves $\$20$ in wholesale cost per unit.

options_template.text: Because profit maximization always requires operating in the inelastic region ($|\varepsilon_d| < 1$) to sell as many units as possible.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inelastic-Profit Fallacy): In the inelastic region, raising price both increases total revenue AND lowers total production cost—so a profit-maximizing firm with positive marginal cost never operates in the inelastic region.

options_template.text: Because Total Revenue is actually minimized rather than maximized at the unit-elastic midpoint.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Extrema Reversal): Along a linear demand curve, the unit-elastic midpoint maximizes Total Revenue; the issue is that profit equals $TR - TC$, not $TR$ alone.

options_template.text: Because raising price slightly above the midpoint reduces output and saves $\$20$ in cost per unit while barely lowering Total Revenue at the flat peak, thereby increasing profit in the elastic region.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At the $TR$ peak, marginal revenue is zero while marginal cost is positive ($\$20$). Raising price into the elastic region lowers cost faster than it lowers revenue, increasing profit ($TR - TC$).

options_template.text: Because cutting price below the midpoint increases both Total Revenue and wholesale costs simultaneously.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inelastic Revenue Direction Error): Cutting price below the midpoint enters the inelastic region where Total Revenue falls while higher volume raises total cost—reducing profit twice over.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Income Elasticity Over the Business Cycle
questions.title: Divergent Demand Responses of Luxuries and Inferior Goods in a Downturn
questions.prompt_template: During a regional recession in which average household incomes decline substantially, how would stylized market demand behave for a luxury vacation package ($\varepsilon_I > 1$) compared with budget store-brand staples classified as an inferior good ($\varepsilon_I < 0$), holding prices constant?

hints.text: Apply the sign of $\varepsilon_I$ when $\%\Delta I < 0$: check whether $\%\Delta Q_d$ is negative or positive for each good.
A falling income multiplies a positive $\varepsilon_I > 1$ into a large percentage drop in demand, but multiplies a negative $\varepsilon_I$ into a positive percentage increase.

options_template.text: Demand for both goods shifts sharply to the left because lower incomes reduce purchases of every product.
