options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (All-Normal Assumption): Inferior goods ($\varepsilon_I < 0$) experience increased—not decreased—demand when incomes fall, as households trade down from pricier alternatives.

options_template.text: Demand for the luxury shifts sharply to the left (falling more than proportionally with income), while demand for the inferior good shifts to the right.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When $\%\Delta I < 0$, $\varepsilon_I > 1$ implies a proportionally larger leftward drop in luxury demand, whereas $\varepsilon_I < 0$ implies a rightward shift toward the inferior good.

options_template.text: Demand for the luxury shifts to the right while demand for the inferior good shifts to the left.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Income-Direction Reversal): This describes the effect of an income expansion ($\%\Delta I > 0$), not a recessionary income decline ($\%\Delta I < 0$).

options_template.text: Demand for the luxury stays unchanged while demand for the inferior good falls proportionally with income.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Elasticity Magnitude & Sign Swap): Luxuries are the most income-sensitive normal goods ($\varepsilon_I > 1$), whereas inferior goods move opposite to income.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Anticipating Transit Capacity Pressure from Higher Parking Fees
questions.prompt_template: A city doubles municipal downtown parking garage rates to reduce car congestion. Suppose downtown parking ($Y$) and commuter rail ($X$) are substitutes ($\varepsilon_{xy} > 0$), and rail seat capacity is nearly fixed in the immediate run ($\varepsilon_s \approx 0$). What combined market outcome should city planners anticipate?

hints.text: First use $\varepsilon_{xy} > 0$ to determine how commuter rail demand shifts when downtown parking prices rise.
Next combine that demand shift with a nearly vertical immediate-run rail supply curve.

options_template.text: Commuter rail demand shifts right; because immediate rail supply is highly inelastic, the system faces peak crowding or upward fare pressure until fleet capacity expands.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher prices for a substitute shift rail demand rightward; with fixed immediate seat capacity ($\varepsilon_s \approx 0$), quantity cannot expand right away, causing crowding or higher equilibrium prices.

options_template.text: Commuter rail demand shifts left because drivers who pay more for parking also take fewer trains.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Substitute-Complement Swap): Higher parking rates reduce rail demand only if the two modes are complements ($\varepsilon_{xy} < 0$), not substitutes ($\varepsilon_{xy} > 0$).

options_template.text: Rail ridership immediately doubles with zero crowding because vertical supply responds instantly to demand shifts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Vertical-Supply Misinterpretation): Vertical supply ($\varepsilon_s = 0$) means zero immediate quantity expansion—not instant doubling of output.

options_template.text: There is no effect on commuter rail because parking fees affect only the automobile market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Isolated-Market Fallacy): Nonzero cross-price elasticity ($\varepsilon_{xy} > 0$) directly links related markets, transmitting price policies from parking to transit.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Semiconductor Price Spikes Moderate Over Longer Time Horizons
questions.prompt_template: In a capacity-intensive industry such as semiconductor fabrication, why does an unexpected surge in global demand typically cause a sharp initial price spike that moderates over a multi-year horizon?

hints.text: Contrast production flexibility immediately after a demand shock with flexibility after new factories can be built.
Connect immediate-run versus long-run supply elasticity to the magnitude of equilibrium price changes.

options_template.text: Because consumer demand becomes completely vertical over a multi-year horizon.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Elasticity Reversal): Demand generally becomes more elastic (flatter)—not vertical—over longer time horizons, and the capacity mechanism here operates through supply.

options_template.text: Because supply is most elastic in the immediate run and grows progressively more inelastic as new factories open.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply Time-Horizon Inversion): Supply elasticity increases—not decreases—as firms gain time to expand factories and enter the market.

options_template.text: Because semiconductor manufacturers voluntarily cut prices after one year even if supply remains completely vertical.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Non-Market Mechanism): In the competitive supply-and-demand framework, price moderation arises from greater long-run supply elasticity and capacity expansion, not arbitrary voluntary cuts.

options_template.text: Because fabrication capacity is nearly fixed in the immediate run (inelastic supply), forcing prices up sharply, whereas multi-year investment and entry flatten supply and moderate prices.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Fixed immediate-run plant capacity yields very low $\varepsilon_s$ and a sharp price jump; over the long run, new fabrication facilities and entry raise $\varepsilon_s$, expanding output and easing prices.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Statutory vs. Economic Tax Incidence in Policy
questions.title: Evaluating Statutory Collection Choices for a Rideshare Excise Fee
questions.prompt_template: A city council proposes a $\$2$ per-trip excise fee on rideshares. One councilmember insists the city must legally collect the fee from rideshare platforms rather than passengers 'so riders will not pay any of the tax.' Under the standard competitive model (assuming equal compliance costs), how should an economist evaluate this claim?

hints.text: Separate statutory incidence (who remits the $\$2$ fee to the city) from economic incidence (how $P_b$ and $P_s$ adjust).
Ask whether changing who writes the check alters the relative elasticities of rider demand and driver supply.

options_template.text: The claim is correct: collecting the fee from platforms prevents passenger fares from rising.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Statutory Incidence Fallacy): When platforms remit a per-unit tax, the supply curve shifts up by $\$2$ and equilibrium passenger fares still rise unless demand is perfectly elastic.

options_template.text: The claim is flawed: statutory collection does not determine economic burden; passenger fare increases vs. lower driver net payouts depend on the relative elasticities of rider demand and driver supply.
options_template.feedback: Correct. In the standard competitive model, the equilibrium wedge ($P_b - P_s = \$2$) and economic incidence are identical regardless of which side legally remits the fee.

options_template.text: The claim is backwards: collecting the fee from platforms actually forces passengers to pay $100\%$ of the fee.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Over-Correction): Collecting from platforms does not automatically force passengers to pay $100\%$ either; the split depends solely on relative elasticities.

options_template.text: The claim is correct only if rider demand is perfectly inelastic ($|\varepsilon_d| = 0$).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Polar-Case Inversion): If rider demand were perfectly inelastic ($|\varepsilon_d| = 0$), passengers would actually pay $100\%$ of the fee—even when collected from platforms.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Empirical Discipline in Cigarette Tax Incidence
questions.title: Evaluating Unsupported Universal Pass-Through Claims for Cigarette Taxes
questions.prompt_template: A commentary asserts: 'Because cigarettes are addictive, demand is always inelastic everywhere, so smokers automatically pay exactly $95\%$ of every cigarette excise tax in any state or country.' Following Chapter 5's empirical discipline, what is the core analytical flaw in this claim?

hints.text: Review Chapter 5's Real-World Application on cigarette excise taxes.
Distinguish a qualitative mechanism (addiction limiting substitutes) from an unsupported universal numerical claim.

options_template.text: Cigarette taxes are legally remitted by distributors, so economic theory proves smokers pay $0\%$ of the tax.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Statutory Incidence Fallacy): Statutory remittance by distributors does not shield consumers from bearing part—or most—of the economic burden.

options_template.text: Addictiveness always makes demand elastic rather than inelastic, so sellers always pay more than $95\%$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Determinant Reversal): Addictiveness tends to limit close substitutes and reduce price sensitivity, not make demand automatically elastic.

options_template.text: While addictiveness may affect available substitutes, it does not establish a universal demand elasticity or exact pass-through rate; quantifying incidence requires empirical evidence on both demand and supply responses in a specific market and period.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Qualitative factors like addictiveness cannot justify a universal pass-through percentage; credible incidence numbers require evidence on both sides of the market for a stated market, time period, and source.

options_template.text: Excise taxes apply only to perfectly competitive markets with zero addiction, so elasticity analysis cannot be used for tobacco.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scope Exclusion Error): Elasticity and tax-incidence tools are routinely applied to cigarette taxes—the key requirement is using market-specific empirical evidence rather than fabricated universal percentages.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Revenue Generation vs. Consumption Reduction Under an Excise Tax
questions.prompt_template: A policymaker compares levying an identical per-unit excise tax $t$ on two markets that have the same pre-tax equilibrium $(Q^*, P^*)$ and identical supply curves: Market A has highly inelastic demand, whereas Market B has highly elastic demand. Which policy trade-off accurately compares the two markets?

hints.text: Compare how much post-tax quantity $Q_t$ shrinks in Market A (steep demand) versus Market B (flat demand).
Tax revenue equals $t \times Q_t$: a smaller drop in $Q_t$ preserves more tax revenue, whereas a larger drop in $Q_t$ achieves greater consumption reduction.

options_template.text: Market A (inelastic demand) generates higher tax revenue with a smaller reduction in quantity traded, whereas Market B (elastic demand) achieves a larger reduction in consumption.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because buyers in Market A barely cut back ($Q_t$ stays close to $Q^*$), tax revenue $t \times Q_t$ is larger; in Market B, buyers walk away in large numbers, shrinking consumption much more.

options_template.text: Market B (elastic demand) generates higher tax revenue because buyers are more responsive to price changes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Base Erosion Oversight): High buyer responsiveness shrinks the post-tax quantity $Q_t$ sharply, eroding the tax base $t \times Q_t$ and lowering tax revenue.

options_template.text: Market A (inelastic demand) produces a larger reduction in consumption because buyers pay a higher post-tax price $P_b$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Jump vs. Quantity-Drop Confusion): Even though $P_b$ rises more in Market A, steep inelastic demand means quantity drops very little compared with flat elastic demand.

options_template.text: Both markets collect identical tax revenue and experience identical quantity drops because the tax $t$ and supply curve are identical.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Invariance Error): Post-tax quantity $Q_t$ depends on both demand and supply elasticities; flatter demand always produces a larger quantity decline for a given tax $t$.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Slopes vs. Relative Elasticities in Tax Incidence
questions.title: Why Raw Curve Slopes Alone Do Not Generally Measure Relative Elasticity
questions.prompt_template: At the end of Section 5.4, Chapter 5 cautions that 'curve slopes alone do not generally measure relative elasticity.' Why can comparing raw slopes across graphs or markets mislead a policy analyst predicting tax incidence?

hints.text: Recall the point elasticity relationship $\varepsilon = (dQ/dP) \cdot (P/Q)$ and how units affect raw slope.
At a single shared intersection $(Q^*, P^*)$ in identical units, $P^*/Q^*$ cancels out; across different markets, price levels, or units, it does not.

options_template.text: Because tax incidence depends only on statutory law and never relates to the slopes of demand or supply.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Statutory Incidence Fallacy): Economic tax incidence is governed by relative elasticities, not statutory law.

options_template.text: Because raw slopes depend on arbitrary measurement units and omit the price-to-quantity ratio ($P/Q$); comparing slopes reflects relative elasticity only at a shared $(Q^*, P^*)$ point measured in the same units.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Elasticity equals $(dQ/dP)\cdot(P/Q)$, which is unit-free; raw slopes change with axis units and ignore $P/Q$, so slope comparisons work only at a common equilibrium point with identical units.

options_template.text: Because linear supply curves always have unit elasticity ($\varepsilon_s = 1$) regardless of their slope or intercept.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Constant-Unit-Supply Myth): Only a linear supply ray passing directly through the origin has $\varepsilon_s = 1$ everywhere; supply curves with positive or negative intercepts do not.

options_template.text: Because a steeper demand curve always has a larger elasticity magnitude $|\varepsilon_d|$ than a flatter demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Steepness-Elasticity Inversion): Through a common point in identical units, a steeper demand curve has a smaller—not larger—elasticity magnitude $|\varepsilon_d|$.
